chain.label: Helicopter returned to service with about 35 percent fuel (~1 hour) instead of the normal 70 percent load
chain.trigger: The Air Methods instructor... reported that he did not have the helicopter refueled after the last flight... Fuel records obtained from the STJ airport manager showed that the helicopter was not refueled on August 26.

chain.label: Pilot fatigued from restricted sleep and long duty/wake period
chain.trigger: his uninterrupted sleep potential was likely limited to no more than about 5 hours... He had been on duty about 12 hours at the time of the accident... and awake more than 13 hours

chain.label: Autorotation training not representative of an actual engine failure at cruise airspeed; no simulator training and guidance emphasizing collective only
chain.trigger: the pilot's autorotation training was done at airspeeds below cruise where less aft cyclic is needed to enter an autorotation... Air Methods elected to conduct practice autorotations with no reduction in throttle... FAA guidance on performing autorotations stresses lowering the collective as the initial step

chain.label: Pilot's nonoperational personal texting during safety-critical ground preparation, in flight, and during the fuel decision call, violating company policy
chain.trigger: the pilot's texting, which occurred (1) while flying, (2) while the helicopter was being prepared for return to service, and (3) during his telephone call to the communication specialist... was a self-induced distraction

chain.label: Pilot failed to detect and confirm the helicopter's low fuel state before the first departure; incomplete preflight, no gauge check, erroneous '2 hours of fuel' report
chain.trigger: although the helicopter's low fuel state was clearly indicated, the pilot missed three opportunities to detect the condition: (1) before departing on the first leg of the mission as a result of his inadequate preflight inspection, (2) before takeoff by failing to properly complete the before-takeoff confirmation checklist, and (3) after takeoff when he erroneously reported the fuel level

caused_by.evidence: Helicopters at the St. Joseph base were normally refueled to about 70 percent following each mission... he might reasonably have expected the normal 70 percent level for an active helicopter
Effects of fatigue on performance include increased lapses (errors of omission)... errors of omission (neglecting to refuel the helicopter and check the fuel gauge before departure)
it is possible that the pilot's nonoperational use of a portable electronic device (PED) contributed to his lack of awareness of the helicopter's abnormally low fuel state

chain.label: Air Methods had no policy requiring notification of the Operational Control Center about abnormal fuel situations and no risk threshold triggering OCC consultation
chain.trigger: At the time of the accident, Air Methods did not require the communication specialist to notify the OCC of fuel-related issues or unplanned deviations... The risk factors listed in the risk assessment matrixes did not include any reference to fuel.

chain.label: Communication specialist never asked how much fuel was on board and did not involve the OCC or chief pilot in the launch decision
chain.trigger: the pilot did not report and the communication specialist did not ask how much fuel was on board the helicopter, and neither of them considered canceling the mission and having fuel brought to the helicopter

caused_by.evidence: because there was no policy requiring that the Air Methods OCC be notified of abnormal fuel situations, available operationally qualified personnel outside the situation... were not consulted

chain.label: Pilot decided to continue the mission and depart with the patient below required fuel reserves, then pressed on to GPH rather than make a precautionary landing
chain.trigger: his improper decision to continue the mission and make a second departure after he became aware of a critically low fuel level... The pilot's decision to continue the flight rather than make a precautionary landing, despite mounting evidence that fuel exhaustion was imminent, was a decision error.

caused_by.evidence: about halfway through the flight from STJ, he had realized that the helicopter did not have as much fuel on board as he originally thought
An operationally qualified individual outside the immediate situation would likely have recognized that the pilot's decision to continue the mission was inappropriate.
the pilot's personal texting activities likely degraded his decision-making performance when he decided to continue the mission
Fatigue degrades decisions involving unexpected situations or plan revision... perseveration on ineffective solutions (continuing the mission after discovering he had insufficient fuel)

chain.label: Flight conducted at low cruise altitude, about 275 feet agl and 115 knots at the time of the flameout
chain.trigger: En route to GPH, the helicopter's altitude averaged between 400 and 600 feet above ground level (agl)... the accident helicopter was at an altitude of about 275 feet agl and an airspeed of about 115 knots when the engine flamed out

chain.label: Engine flamed out from fuel exhaustion about 1 nm short of the airport
chain.trigger: The evidence was consistent with a loss of engine power due to fuel exhaustion occurring shortly before impact... the engine was flamed out when impact occurred

caused_by.evidence: Wreckage examination determined that the engine lost power due to fuel exhaustion and that the fuel system was operating properly.
the pilot departed on the second leg of the mission despite knowing that the helicopter had insufficient fuel reserves

chain.label: Pilot did not make the simultaneous aft cyclic and down collective inputs needed to enter an autorotation
chain.trigger: the pilot did not make the flight control inputs necessary to enter an autorotation, which resulted in a rapid decay in rotor rpm

caused_by.evidence: his failure to successfully enter an autorotation when the engine lost power due to fuel exhaustion

the autorotation training that the pilot received in the Eurocopter AS350 B2 was not representative of an actual engine failure at cruise airspeed and likely contributed to the pilot's failure to execute a successful autorotation

chain.label: Rapid rotor rpm decay and nose-down, high-rate uncontrolled descent
chain.trigger: if these flight control inputs were not made within about 1 to 2 seconds, the helicopter's nose dropped, the rotor rpm decayed rapidly, and the helicopter impacted terrain about 4 to 5 seconds after the unannounced loss of power

caused_by.evidence: the pilot failed to make the flight control inputs necessary to enter an autorotation when the engine lost power, which resulted in a rapid decay in rotor rpm and impact with terrain
this condition may be unrecoverable at low altitudes

chain.label: Helicopter impacted a farm field in a 40 degree nose-down attitude at a high rate of descent with low rotor rpm
chain.trigger: The helicopter impacted the ground in about a 40 degree nose-down attitude at a high rate of descent with a low rotor rpm... the wreckage was located... in a farm field about 1 nm from the approach end of runway 18

caused_by.evidence: The wreckage displayed vertical crush damage consistent with impact at a high rate of descent... consistent with a low rotor rpm at impact.

chain.label: Pilot, flight nurse, flight paramedic, and patient fatally injured
chain.trigger: The pilot, flight nurse, flight paramedic, and patient were killed, and the helicopter was substantially damaged by impact forces.

caused_by.evidence: were killed, and the helicopter was substantially damaged by impact forces
